input:
Scope

This review is concerned with adsorbents for gas drying, that is to say, with the removal of water vapour from a process gas by means of adsorption on a solid, down to a dew point that is determined by the requirements of the duty downstream. In total, the review covers 154 papers that have been published over the last 11 years. The materials that are covered are the three classes that are in industrial use for this duty, namely silica gel, activated alumina, and zeolite molecular sieves. The papers are drawn from the journal and conference literature in the fields of adsorption and gas processing, and the review is limited specifically to drying. Work dealing with the removal of acid gases, hydrocarbons, or other contaminants is included only in those cases where the same bed is also used to dry the gas and the behaviour of the water is reported in its own right. Studies of water isotherms, of mixed-gas breakthrough, and of cyclic operation are all regarded as falling inside the scope of the review, since the design questions to which they provide answers are different from one another and a drying bed must be specified against all three of them. The review does not cover liquid desiccants, membrane drying, or refrigeration drying, nor does it attempt to reanalyse the primary data; instead, the reported values are compared as they are published, with the measurement method being stated in those cases where the method has a bearing on the comparison. Two terms are used throughout the review in fixed senses. Capacity denotes the water uptake of the adsorbent at the stated partial pressure and temperature, expressed per unit mass of adsorbent. Regeneration denotes the removal of the water that has been adsorbed in order to restore the capacity, whether this is achieved by means of a heated purge, by pressure reduction, or by a combination of the two.

Established results

The relative behaviour of the three classes at low water partial pressure is not a matter of dispute. Zeolite molecular sieves take up more water than either silica gel or activated alumina at low partial pressure, and a bed of zeolite material is able to maintain the driest outlet of the three classes; the zeolite isotherm is characterised by a steep rise at low partial pressure followed by an early flattening, so that most of its capacity is available in precisely the region where the duty is driest. Silica gel, by contrast, takes up the greatest amount of water of the three classes in the region near to saturation, and it is used in situations where the feed is wet and the specification on the outlet is moderate; its isotherm rises late, and its capacity is found to fall steeply as the temperature is increased. Activated alumina occupies an intermediate position between the two in terms of affinity, is tolerant of liquid water being carried into the bed, and is widely employed as a guard layer ahead of a sieve bed for this reason. The capacity of every class falls as the temperature rises, which is because adsorption is an exothermic process, and a bed warms as the adsorption step proceeds, with the result that the working isotherm of a bed in service lies below the isotherm that is measured under constant temperature conditions. Regeneration by means of a heated purge, in the temperature-swing arrangement, represents the standard route for deep drying duties, while regeneration by pressure reduction alone is used for smaller duties where the specification on the outlet is less demanding. The severity of regeneration that each class requires follows its affinity, in that the zeolites, which hold water the most strongly, require the most severe regeneration, and silica gel requires the least. The capacity that a bed is able to deliver in cyclic service is lower than its equilibrium capacity, because the mass-transfer zone occupies a part of the bed at breakthrough and that part is not used to its equilibrium loading; breakthrough curves obtained from beds of every class show the presence of the zone, and it is standard design practice to size the bed on the basis of the working capacity rather than the equilibrium figure. Ageing is likewise a matter of common ground in outline: capacity declines over the course of repeated cycling as a result of hydrothermal damage to the structure, contamination of the pores by heavier species that are present in the feed, and attrition of the particles, and this decline is at its fastest during the early life of a charge.

Disagreements

The reports in the literature conflict on the subject of the equilibrium water uptake at low partial pressure, and this conflict represents the largest open disagreement that was identified in the course of the review. For one and the same class of material, and in some reports for one and the same commercial grade, the published values of uptake at a given low partial pressure differ from one another by amounts that are larger than the scatter that the authors themselves report within their own measurements. In what follows, the review weighs the methods that lie behind the values before it weighs the values themselves. Part of the spread can be traced to the pretreatment that is applied, since the temperature and duration of the drying step that precedes the measurement, together with the vacuum or purge that is applied, are not the same between laboratories, and a material that has been measured after only a mild pretreatment will carry residual water into the measurement and will accordingly report a lower uptake. A further part can be traced to the method of measurement. Gravimetric and volumetric measurements carried out on the same material do not always agree with one another, and capacities that are derived from breakthrough curves conflate the equilibrium uptake with the kinetics of the bed, so that a figure derived from breakthrough is not an equilibrium measurement and is given a correspondingly lower weight here. A further part follows from the basis on which the results are reported: uptake per unit mass of dry adsorbent and uptake per unit volume of bed both appear in the literature, sometimes within one and the same journal, and the two are not converted into one another in those cases where the bulk density is not stated. The preference of this review is for direct equilibrium measurements in which the pretreatment is stated, and the disagreement is accordingly recorded as unresolved in respect of values that rest on an unstated pretreatment or on a breakthrough derivation.

Gaps

The measurement that nobody reports is the water uptake that is retained after extended regeneration cycling. Papers report the capacity of a fresh charge, and many of them also report its capacity after a short series of cycles carried out under mild regeneration conditions, but the uptake of a charge after prolonged cycling under the severity of regeneration that is characteristic of an industrial dryer is absent from the literature that this review covers. This absence is of considerable importance, because the quantity that matters for design purposes is not the fresh capacity: a dryer is specified on the basis of the capacity that the charge still retains late in its working life, and the replacement of the charge is scheduled on the basis of the same figure. In the absence of the measurement, it is the practice in design to extrapolate from the decline observed over short cycling, and this extrapolation is not checked against the long-cycle behaviour for which it stands as a substitute. The same absence also conceals the interaction between ageing and the severity of regeneration, since a charge that is regenerated more severely retains more of its capacity in each cycle but at the same time loses capacity more rapidly as a result of structural damage, and no report within the review separates these two effects from one another over a long run of operation. The gap is therefore identified here as a gap in measurement rather than a gap in modelling, in that the quantity in question is measurable with existing apparatus over the timescale of an extended experimental campaign, and it is its absence from the record that constitutes the finding.

Scope

Regeneration means the removal of the adsorbed water to restore capacity, by heated purge, by pressure reduction, or by both together.

Where a paper reports both a fresh capacity and a cycled capacity, both values enter the record, and the review keeps the two apart throughout: fresh and cycled values are never combined into a single figure for a material, because the design questions they answer are different and a combined figure answers neither.

Established results

The relative behaviour of the three classes at low water partial pressure is not in dispute. Zeolite molecular sieves take up more water than silica gel or activated alumina at low partial pressure, and a zeolite bed holds the driest outlet of the three; the zeolite isotherm rises steeply at low partial pressure and flattens early, so most of its capacity is available where the duty is driest. Silica gel takes up the most water of the three near saturation and is used where the feed is wet and the outlet specification moderate; its isotherm rises late, and its capacity falls steeply as the temperature rises. Activated alumina stands between the two in affinity, is tolerant of liquid water carried into the bed, and is widely used as a guard layer ahead of a sieve bed for that reason. The capacity of every class falls as the temperature rises, because adsorption is exothermic, and a bed warms as the adsorption step proceeds, so the working isotherm of a bed in service sits below the isotherm measured at constant temperature. Regeneration by a heated purge, in the temperature-swing arrangement, is the standard route for deep drying; regeneration by pressure reduction alone serves smaller duties where the outlet specification is less severe. The regeneration severity each class needs follows its affinity: the zeolites, holding water most strongly, need the most severe regeneration, and silica gel the least. The capacity a bed delivers in cyclic service is lower than its equilibrium capacity, because the mass-transfer zone occupies part of the bed at breakthrough and that part is not used to its equilibrium loading; breakthrough curves from beds of every class show the zone, and design practice sizes the bed on the working capacity, not on the equilibrium figure. Ageing is likewise common ground in outline: capacity declines over repeated cycling through hydrothermal damage to the structure, through contamination of the pores by heavier species in the feed, and through attrition of the particles, and the decline is fastest in the early life of a charge.

Industrial drying practice reflects the ordering. A wet feed is taken first over activated alumina or silica gel, which carry the bulk of the water in the region where capacity near saturation is what counts, and the gas is finished over a sieve bed, which carries the duty in the region where the isotherm of the gel has already flattened. The layered bed is the standard arrangement the literature describes, and it assigns to each class the part of the isotherm on which that class is strongest. The same ordering governs the choice for a single-bed duty: the class is selected by the outlet dryness the duty demands, and the capacity at the feed condition is checked afterwards, not the other way round.

Disagreements

Reports conflict on the equilibrium water uptake at low partial pressure, and the conflict is the largest open disagreement the review found. For the same class of material, and in some reports for the same commercial grade, published uptakes at a given low partial pressure differ by amounts that exceed the scatter the authors report within their own measurements. The review weighs the methods behind the values before the values themselves. Part of the spread follows the pretreatment: the temperature and duration of the drying step before measurement, and the vacuum or purge applied, differ between laboratories, and a material measured after a mild pretreatment carries residual water into the measurement and reports a lower uptake. Part follows the method. Gravimetric and volumetric measurements of the same material do not always agree, and capacities derived from breakthrough curves conflate the equilibrium uptake with the kinetics of the bed, so a breakthrough-derived figure is not an equilibrium measurement and is weighted accordingly here. Part follows the reporting basis: uptake per unit mass of dry adsorbent and uptake per unit volume of bed both appear in the literature, sometimes in the same journal, and the two are not converted into one another where the bulk density is not stated. The preference of this review is for direct equilibrium measurements with the pretreatment stated, and the disagreement is recorded as unresolved on values that rest on unstated pretreatment or on breakthrough derivation.

The conflict is sharpest at the lowest partial pressures, where the sieve isotherm is at its steepest and a small difference in the state of the sample moves the measured uptake by the most. Reports on silica gel agree more closely, because the gel isotherm is flat in the region where the sieve isotherm rises, and the same difference in pretreatment moves the gel uptake by less. The disagreement is therefore not evenly spread over the record: it concentrates on the materials and the region that deep drying depends on.

Gaps

The measurement nobody reports is the water uptake retained after extended regeneration cycling. Papers report the capacity of a fresh charge, and many report its capacity after a short series of cycles under mild regeneration, but the uptake of a charge after long cycling under the regeneration severity of an industrial dryer is absent from the literature the review covers. The absence matters because the design quantity is not the fresh capacity: a dryer is specified on the capacity the charge still holds late in its life, and replacement of the charge is scheduled from the same figure. In the absence of the measurement, design practice extrapolates the short-cycle decline, and the extrapolation is unchecked against the long-cycle behaviour it stands for. The same absence hides the interaction between ageing and regeneration severity: a charge regenerated harder keeps more of its capacity per cycle and loses capacity faster to structural damage, and no report in the review separates the two effects over a long run. The gap is therefore stated as a measurement gap, not as a modelling gap: the quantity is measurable with existing apparatus, over the timescale of a long experimental campaign, and its absence from the record is the finding.

Until the measurement exists, the ranking of materials for long service rests on fresh capacity and on short cycling, which are the quantities the disagreements section shows to be unsettled at low partial pressure. A material selected on fresh capacity alone is selected on the figure least representative of the duty it will serve, and the review records that consequence as part of the gap.
